frontmatter.title: How Learning Rate Shapes the Journey of a Small CNN

children.value: Deep learning portfolio post · Fashion-MNIST · PyTorch Lightning
Every neural network tutorial tells you to “tune the learning rate”, and every beginner (me included) nods and moves on. But what does the learning rate actually
to training? Does a bigger one just mean faster? Does a smaller one just mean safer?

When I train the same small convolutional network on the same data with plain SGD, how does the learning rate change the shape of the training and validation curves, and which value gives the best validation accuracy within a fixed 15-epoch budget?
I will explain the idea first, then test four learning rates in a controlled experiment.
η = 0.001 was smooth but slow, η = 0.01 and 0.1 were faster but noisy, and η = 1.0 collapsed into guessing. η = 0.1 won, with 85.1% validation accuracy after 15 epochs.

Picture walking down a foggy hill. You can feel the slope under your feet but cannot see the valley. The learning rate is how long your stride is:
you shuffle downhill safely but painfully slowly. With a fixed number of epochs you may simply run out of time before reaching a good spot.
you descend quickly and settle near the bottom.
you overshoot the valley floor and land on the opposite slope, higher than where you started. The loss bounces around, or even explodes to
So the learning rate controls both
, and those two pull in opposite directions. That tension is why it is often called the most important hyperparameter.

import logging, warnings
import torch, torch.nn as nn, torch.nn.functional as F
import lightning as L
from lightning.pytorch.loggers import CSVLogger
from torch.utils.data import DataLoader, TensorDataset, random_split
from torchvision import datasets, transforms

BATCH_SIZE = 64

tfm  = transforms.Compose([transforms.ToTensor(), transforms.Normalize((0.2860,), (0.3530,))])
full = datasets.FashionMNIST("data", train=True, download=True, transform=tfm)

g = torch.Generator().manual_seed(SEED)
train_ds, val_ds, _ = random_split(full, [N_TRAIN, N_VAL, len(full) - N_TRAIN - N_VAL], generator=g)
def to_gpu(ds):
    # The subset is tiny (15k images, ~47 MB), so keep it on the GPU: no CPU->GPU copies during training
    xs = torch.stack([ds[i][0] for i in range(len(ds))]).to(DEVICE)
    ys = torch.tensor([ds[i][1] for i in range(len(ds))]).to(DEVICE)
    return TensorDataset(xs, ys)

train_ds, val_ds = to_gpu(train_ds), to_gpu(val_ds)
print(len(train_ds), "train images,", len(val_ds), "validation images, stored on", train_ds.tensors[0].device)

import glob, os, gc

def load_latest(lr):
    # Return the per-epoch metrics of the newest *complete* run for this lr from logs/, else None
    paths = sorted(glob.glob(f"logs/lr_{lr}/version_*/metrics.csv"), key=os.path.getmtime, reverse=True)
    for p in paths:
        m = pd.read_csv(p).groupby("epoch").first().reset_index()   # merge train/val rows per epoch
        if len(m) == EPOCHS and m["val_acc"].notna().all():
            return m
    return None

# Resumable: a finished run is reloaded from logs/ instead of retrained, so a kernel crash never costs you results.
# If you change any setting (batch size, epochs, model...), delete the logs/ folder first.
curves = {}
for lr in LRS:
    done = load_latest(lr)
    if done is not None:
        curves[lr] = done
        print(f"lr={lr}: reusing finished run from logs/ (final val_acc = {done['val_acc'].iloc[-1]:.4f})")
        continue

    L.seed_everything(SEED, workers=True)
    # num_workers=0 / no pin_memory: the data already lives on the GPU
    train_dl = DataLoader(train_ds, batch_size=BATCH_SIZE, shuffle=True)
    val_dl   = DataLoader(val_ds,   batch_size=256)
    logger   = CSVLogger("logs", name=f"lr_{lr}")
    trainer  = L.Trainer(max_epochs=EPOCHS, logger=logger, enable_checkpointing=False,
                         enable_progress_bar=False, enable_model_summary=False, accelerator="gpu", devices=1)
    model = SmallCNN(lr)
    trainer.fit(model, train_dl, val_dl)

    curves[lr] = load_latest(lr)
    print(f"lr={lr}: final val_acc = {curves[lr]['val_acc'].iloc[-1]:.4f}")

    # Free GPU objects before the next run
    del trainer, model, train_dl, val_dl, logger
    gc.collect(); torch.cuda.empty_cache()

%matplotlib inline
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

LOSS_CAP = 5.0   # random guessing on 10 classes gives ln(10) ≈ 2.30, so 5 is already "broken"

def clean_loss(series):
    v = np.array(pd.to_numeric(series, errors="coerce"), dtype=float)   # np.array makes a writable copy
    v[~np.isfinite(v)] = np.nan          # inf/NaN -> gap in the line
    return np.clip(v, 1e-3, LOSS_CAP)    # huge values -> capped (NaN stays NaN)
    
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4.5))
for lr, c in curves.items():
    ep = c["epoch"].to_numpy() + 1
    line, = axes[0].plot(ep, clean_loss(c["val_loss"]), label=f"lr={lr} (val)")
    axes[0].plot(ep, clean_loss(c["train_loss"]), "--", color=line.get_color(), label=f"lr={lr} (train)")
    axes[1].plot(ep, c["val_acc"].to_numpy(dtype=float), label=f"lr={lr}")

axes[0].set_xlabel("Epoch"); axes[0].set_ylabel(f"Cross-entropy loss (capped at {LOSS_CAP})")
axes[0].set_title("Loss per epoch"); axes[0].set_yscale("log"); axes[0].set_ylim(0.2, LOSS_CAP * 1.2)
axes[0].legend(fontsize=7, ncol=2); axes[0].grid(alpha=.3)
axes[1].set_xlabel("Epoch"); axes[1].set_ylabel("Validation accuracy")
axes[1].set_title("Validation accuracy per epoch"); axes[1].legend(); axes[1].grid(alpha=.3)

plt.tight_layout()
fig.savefig("learning_curves.png", dpi=150)
plt.show()

Training loss (dashed) and validation loss (solid), log scale (left), and validation accuracy (right), per epoch for each learning rate. Losses are capped at 5 for plotting; no run actually reached that value.

Figure 1 shows that the three learning rates that learned are clearly separated: after the first epoch η = 0.1 was at about 71% validation accuracy, η = 0.01 at about 63% and η = 0.001 at about 34%, while η = 1.0 stayed flat near 10%. It also shows that the η = 0.01 and η = 0.1 validation curves are jagged, whereas the η = 0.001 curves are smooth.

rows = []
for lr, c in curves.items():
    best = c["val_acc"].idxmax()
    rows.append({
        "learning rate": lr,
        "final train loss": c["train_loss"].iloc[-1],
        "final val loss":   c["val_loss"].iloc[-1],
        "final val acc":    c["val_acc"].iloc[-1],
        "best val acc":     c["val_acc"].max(),
        "best epoch":       int(c["epoch"].iloc[best]) + 1,
    })
table = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("learning rate")
table.round(4)

children.value: Final-epoch and best-epoch results for the four runs (single seed, 15 epochs, validation set). “Best val acc” is the highest of the 15 per-epoch values, so it is picked on the validation set itself and is slightly optimistic; the final-epoch number is the fairer comparison.

Table 1 shows that η = 0.1 is best on every accuracy and loss column: 85.1% final validation accuracy against 80.5% for η = 0.01 (4.6 percentage points higher), and 88.8% at its best epoch against 84.1%. η = 0.001 reached 75.4% and η = 1.0 only 10.2%.

Three learning rates learned and one did not. With η = 0.001 the curves are smooth and training and validation loss almost overlap (0.694 vs. 0.683), but learning was slow: validation accuracy climbed from about 34% to 75.4% and training loss was still falling at epoch 15.

η = 0.01 and η = 0.1 learned much faster (about 63% and 71% after epoch 1) and finished at 80.5% and 85.1%. Their validation curves are jagged, though: validation loss spikes at epochs 3 and 6 for both, while the dashed training loss falls smoothly. Both peaked at epoch 13 (84.1% and 88.8%) and ended 3.6 and 3.7 points below that peak.

η = 1.0 never learned. Its training loss averaged 1.94 in epoch 1, below the 2.30 of random guessing, so it started to learn. From epoch 2 on both losses sit at about 2.31 and validation accuracy stays between 9.5% and 10.5%. Giving all 10 classes equal probability yields loss ln(10) ≈ 2.303, so the network had collapsed into guessing. The loss never became

Predictions 1 and 3 were right: η = 0.001 was smooth, slow and still improving, and η = 0.1 was fastest and best. Prediction 2 was only partly right: η = 0.01 made progress, but not “steadily”, because its validation curve was noisy. Prediction 4 was partly wrong: η = 1.0 failed by getting stuck at chance level, not by exploding.

It fits the step-size picture. Tiny steps make smooth but slow progress. Larger steps are faster, but each comes from a noisy 64-image mini-batch and can overshoot, so the weights bounce around the valley floor. Validation is measured at one instant per epoch and catches the bounce; the training loss is averaged over the whole epoch and hides it. For η = 1.0 one huge step can throw the weights somewhere the gradient cannot lead back from, perhaps by switching off most ReLU units (“dead” units), but I did not check this.

At epoch 15 the gap is 0.21 vs. 0.49 for η = 0.1 and 0.40 vs. 0.63 for η = 0.01, whereas η = 0.001 has none and is still underfit. Because of the jitter I cannot tell overfitting from noise: validation loss does not rise steadily, and for η = 0.1 it reaches about 0.3 at epoch 13 before jumping back up.
Epoch-to-epoch swings of 3 to 8 points for η = 0.01 and 0.1 are comparable to some differences I discuss; I would want several seeds before trusting the 4.6-point gap between them.
My values are 10× apart, so the best learning rate may lie between 0.1 and 1.0.
Plain SGD, tiny model, 10k images, 15 epochs.
The results may not transfer to Adam, bigger networks or longer training.

The useful learning-rate range is narrow.

Across two orders of magnitude the result went from slow (0.001: 75.4%) to best (0.1: 85.1%) to a network that could not learn (1.0: 10.2%). Search on a log scale and test just below the point where training breaks.
